description: A biome is a world of its own: rainforest, dry zone, highland or coast, each changing in its own way. We are Biome, taking on “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” at NASA Space Apps 2026 in Kandy. We’re building a tool that lets students and the public pick a place and a question, then see what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the trend is statistically significant, using 25 years of NASA rainfall, vegetation, temperature and soil moisture data.
summary:
Last November, Cyclone Ditwah killed 638 people in Sri Lanka, 234 of them in Kandy. Earlier this year, 23,000 families lived on trucked water during a drought. NASA's satellites saw both coming. The families under them did not.

Biome is an Earth system trend detective for Sri Lanka. It reads free NASA data going back to 1980 (GPM IMERG rain, GLDAS soil moisture, MERRA-2, MODIS vegetation and NASADEM terrain) for all 25 districts and 330 divisions. It turns that data into simple warnings in Sinhala, Tamil and English. Families get a daily Yellow, Amber or Red level and the nearest safer place to go. Farmers get a seasonal outlook telling them when to plant and when to save tank water. Officers can see which districts are on DryWatch, FloodWatch or SlopeWatch.

We tested Biome on past disasters. It would have put Kandy on SlopeWatch a month before Ditwah, and it caught the 2016 Aranayake landslide. It runs by itself on GitHub Actions and sends Telegram alerts. It needs no server, no new sensors and no new budget. Biome helps make sure the next storm finds us ready.
details:
WHAT BIOME DOES

Biome is a free website and Telegram alert service. It turns NASA Earth data into plain warnings for every one of Sri Lanka's 25 districts and 330 divisions, in Sinhala, Tamil and English. Each group it protects has its own page:

- Families: today's risk level (Yellow, Amber or Red), the current Watch, and the nearest safer buildings, each checked for slope and flood risk.

- Farmers: a 12-month outlook, a planting card for the Maha and Yala seasons, and live reservoir (tank) levels.

- Coast: flood warnings for the coastal districts.

Every report answers plain questions such as "Is it safe at home today?" and "Should I plant now?", and shows NASA satellite pictures of that district. Officers get an overview of all 25 districts sorted by risk. A year plan prints on A4 with QR codes for village noticeboards. Anyone can sign up on Telegram to get an alert in their own language when their district reaches the level they choose.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data: with NASA Earthdata Login and the earthaccess library, we stream only the Sri Lanka area of each file. Each satellite grid cell is weighted by how much of it lies inside each district and division.

2. Normals: rain is measured as a percentage of the 2001 to 2025 normal for that month. Ground wetness is ranked against the same month in other years.

3. Three Watches:

- DryWatch: 3-month rain at or below 75% of normal, on ground in the driest 25%.

- FloodWatch: rain at or above 150% of normal, on ground in the wettest 25%.

- SlopeWatch: rain at or above 130% of normal, on ground in the wettest 25%, in hill country. Hill country is measured, not assumed: 10% or more of the land is steeper than 15 degrees in NASADEM.

4. Daily levels from IMERG Early and Late rain:

- Yellow at 75 mm in a day, or when a Watch is on.

- Amber at 100 mm, or 75 mm on soaked ground.

- Red at 150 mm, or 100 mm on soaked ground.

5. Outlook: a weighted analog ensemble. Every year since 1980 is one possible future, weighted by how close its ocean state (NOAA Oceanic Nino Index) was to today's. The kernel width is chosen by cross-validation. Skill is tested by leaving each year out and scoring the forecast with the ranked probability skill score.

6. Trend detection: seasonal Mann-Kendall tests with Sen's slope, a Benjamini-Hochberg correction because 25 districts are tested at once, and permutation tests against 5,000 random sets of years.

7. Automation: GitHub Actions runs the whole pipeline on a schedule with no server. NASA data and analysis run daily, IMERG Early rain and live gauges every 3 hours, NASA pictures daily, and MODIS weekly.

WHAT WE FOUND AND HOW WE VALIDATED IT

- Past disasters: we tested Biome on three real events and it caught two. It would have put Kandy on SlopeWatch in October 2025, a month before Cyclone Ditwah. It caught the 2016 Aranayake landslide. It missed the 2017 Ratnapura floods, which came from one extreme day after a dry month. Monthly data cannot see that kind of event, and we say so on the site.

- Ground truth: IMERG rain matches NOAA GHCN ground rain gauges with a correlation of 0.85 or more at four of five stations. Nuwara Eliya, in the mountains, is lower at 0.5.

- El Nino memory: after every one of the six past strong El Ninos, January to March brought only 30 to 50% of normal rain. The result is significant in 20 of 25 districts. For Maha 2026/27, Biome gives a 7 in 10 chance of a drier than usual season, with drought danger peaking in January. Reservoirs should hold water after these floods.

WHO BENEFITS

Biome is built for the people who protect communities: agriculture extension officers, Disaster Management Centre and NBRO officers, Divisional Secretariats, journalists and teachers. Through them it reaches the farmer deciding when to plant and the family on a hillside deciding when to leave home. It is free, works on a phone, and speaks the user's language.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- One tool covers drought, flood and landslide together, because they hit the same districts and the same families months apart.

- It works at division level, not only district level, and points to real safer buildings checked against NASA terrain.

- Every number shows which NASA dataset it came from.

- It costs nothing to run: free NASA data, free hosting and scheduled automation.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED AND HONEST LIMITS

- Satellite rain is coarse (about 10 km), so it can miss a single hillside.

- NASA rain arrives about 4 to 14 hours after it falls, so a daily level describes the day just gone.

- The outlook gives chances, not certainties, and rests on a small number of past strong El Ninos.

- Biome does not replace official warnings. Every page points to the Department of Meteorology, NBRO and the Disaster Management Centre (117).

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

- Python: xarray, pandas, numpy, scipy, earthaccess.

- Website: Vite, JavaScript, d3-geo and Observable Plot (classic view); React, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui and Recharts (dashboard).

- Automation and hosting: GitHub Actions, Vercel, GitHub Pages.

- Alerts: Telegram Bot API.

- Code: https://github.com/PasinduSuraweera/biome

WHAT'S NEXT

- Test every Watch against NBRO and DMC disaster records back to 2001.

- Run a pilot with Kandy district officers, starting from SLIIT Kandy UNI: SMS alerts, and safe centres checked on site.

- Add NBRO slope maps and coastline change.
